newsitem.title: USA: U.S. trade gap soars, puts spotlight on China.
newsitem.headline: U.S. trade gap soars, puts spotlight on China.

text.p: The trade deficit jumped unexpectedly in September as exports fell and imports of costly oil rose, the government said Wednesday, pointing to slower economic growth in the latter part of the year.
The deficit jumped 10 percent in September to $11.34 billion from a revised $10.30 billion in August, the Commerce Department said.

That capped the nation's worst third-quarter trade performance in nine years, marked by a steadily mounting deficit with China, which surpassed Japan during the quarter as the biggest contributor to the overall trade gap.

Exports fell 1.4 percent to $68.79 billion while imports grew 0.1 percent to $80.13 billion. The total deficit of $33.2 billion for July through September was the highest since a $38.6 billion trade gap in the third quarter of 1987.

Economist Joel Naroff of First Union Corp. in Charlotte, N.C., described the deterioration in September trade as "a truly pathetic performance" and warned that the situation with China was becoming critical.

Secretary of State Warren Christopher met Chinese officials in Beijing Wednesday and President Bill Clinton was to meet Chinese President Jiang Zemin on Sunday as leaders met at an Asia-Pacific economic summit in the Philippines.

Once again in September, the deficit with China was bigger than with any other country. It rose 0.4 percent from August to $4.73 billion. The third-quarter deficit with China grew to $13.3 billion, exceeding the $11.9 billion gap with Japan.

Analysts said the drop in September exports meant the economy was probably weaker in the third quarter than had been thought. They said the economy probably grew at a 1.8 percent rate in the quarter, compared with the Commerce Department's previous estimate of 2.2 percent growth. The economy grew at a brisk 4.7 percent rate in the second quarter.
"Net exports is going to be a bit more of a drag (on the economy) than what was estimated initially," said Chris Iggo, chief economist at BZW Securities Inc.
"This will further constrain an expansion that is already looking at the possibility of softer consumer demand," First Union's Naroff said.
Economists polled by Reuters, on average, had expected the September trade gap to narrow to $9.5 billion.
The National Association of Manufacturers warned that the dollar's appreciation against other currencies was making American-made goods too costly for foreigners.
"The current level of the dollar is preventing the expected boom in U.S. exports," Jerry Jasinowski, president of the manufacturers' group, said in Washington on Tuesday.

Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor blamed September's soft trade performance on sluggish economies in Europe, Canada and Japan. Kantor, who is leaving the top Commerce post, also said the United States "must continue to assign great importance to the Chinese" and make them meet international agreements.

The trade report initially sent the dollar lower, as traders bet that Washington might try to bring the currency lower to help make American exports more competitive. But the dollar regained most of the lost ground by midday.

Imports of petroleum products jumped 9.3 percent in September to $5.97 billion. The price per barrel of imported crude oil hit $20.02, up from $18.65 in August, and the highest since the $22.98 a barrel reached in January 1991 during the Gulf War against Iraq.
As a result, the monthly deficit with oil-producing OPEC countries soared 27.8 percent to $2.2 billion in September, the highest since November 1990.
Foreign sales of civilian aircraft tumbled to $760 million in September from $1.35 billion in August. Analysts had said shipments of aircraft by Boeing Co. would fall in September.
The deficit with Western Europe fell 33.6 percent to $1.04 billion from $1.56 billion in August. The deficit with Canada narrowed to $2.02 billion from $2.38 billion in August.
